column2: Trying to Be Pure Consciousness Is Tiring
Ajahn Pasanno answers questions from visitors during the Monday night gathering at Three Jewels, a small branch of Abhayagiri on the California coast.

column6: Session title

Luang Por, did you sleep okay last night?
Reed Perry sleeps on Eurorail trains while travelling with friends.
Ajahn Pasanno falls asleep while holding a book.
{teachers} compares his experience of Buddhism at university with that of a Three Jewels visitor.

Intellectually I understand and can observe the illusion my eye presents, and I can detach from it. But at 3am, when I wake up and something comes into my mind, I really attach. It's like everything I learned is out the window. I try to remind myself that it's temporary and impermanent and try not to get involved. Any suggestions?
Sometimes a thought will completely wipe out [my perception] of my whole body.
What about pure consciousness?
Ud 8.3: Nibbāna Sutta.
Trying to be pure consciousness is tiring.
The Buddha points to the simplicity of mind where there is the possibility of freedom.
So we are consciousness as opposed to having consciousness?
I find that there's a lot of overlap between cognitive behavioral skills and meditation and Buddhism.
I notice that I would go after something like getting a degree, but after I got there, the excitement dissipated. Any suggestions on being present in the moment?
Desire is not quenchable.
